claims.statement: Jane Austen was born at the Rectory in Steventon, a village in north-east Hampshire, on 16 December 1775, the seventh child and second daughter of the rector, the Revd George Austen, and his wife Cassandra (née Leigh).

Steventon Rectory was her home for the first 25 years of her life; after some years in Bath and Southampton she moved in 1809 with her mother and sister to a cottage at Chawton, on one of her brother Edward's Hampshire estates, where she revised her early novels and wrote Mansfield Park, Emma and Persuasion.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Anchors the modern home and work history.

claims.statement: Her only sister, Cassandra, like Jane herself, never married.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Anchors the modern social history; she has no children.

claims.statement: In 1783, as a young child at school in Southampton with her sister, she caught a putrid fever and was very ill and nearly died.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Past history only; not used as a modern diagnosis.

claims.statement: The chronology in the 1913 family biography dates the first break in her health to about March 1816.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The anchor for the index visit and the synthetic presenting illness.

source_links.locator: Jane's health began to break about this time

claims.statement: In May 1816 she and Cassandra spent three weeks at Cheltenham, stopping at Steventon and at Kintbury on the way; the family biographers judged that she 'must have been decidedly out of health, for the change in her did not escape the notice of her friends.'
claims.clinical_interpretation: After the index date. No modern visit is placed in May or June.

claims.statement: She wrote 'Finis' at the end of the first draft of Persuasion on 18 July 1816; the family memoir quoted in the 1913 biography speaks of the weak state of her health at the time.
claims.clinical_interpretation: After the index date; recorded as history.

claims.statement: In a letter to Cassandra on 8 September 1816 she wrote: 'Thank you, my back has given me scarcely any pain for many days. I have an idea that agitation does it as much harm as fatigue, and that I was ill at the time of your going from the very circumstance of your going.'
claims.clinical_interpretation: After the index date; her own account of back pain and fatigue, echoed in the synthetic presenting symptoms.

claims.statement: On 20 February 1817 she wrote to her niece Fanny Knight that she was 'almost entirely cured of my rheumatism—just a little pain in my knee, now and then'.
claims.clinical_interpretation: After the index date; recorded as history.

claims.statement: On 23 March 1817 she wrote to Fanny Knight: 'I certainly have not been well for many weeks, and about a week ago I was very poorly. I have had a good deal of fever at times, and indifferent nights; but I am considerably better now and am recovering my looks a little, which have been bad enough—black and white and every wrong colour.'
claims.clinical_interpretation: After the index date; her own description of her colour, on which the Addison's disease interpretation rests.

source_links.locator: black and white, and every wrong color

claims.statement: On 6 April 1817 she wrote to her brother Charles that she had been 'suffering from a bilious attack attended with a good deal of fever', that she lived upstairs for the present, and that she was not strong enough to travel except in a closed carriage.
claims.clinical_interpretation: After the index date; recorded as history.

claims.statement: Her niece Caroline, who saw her in the spring of 1817, recalled that she was very pale, her voice weak and low, with 'a general appearance of debility and suffering', and had been told that she never had much acute pain.
claims.clinical_interpretation: After the index date; recorded as history.

claims.statement: On 24 May 1817 she moved to Winchester to be under the care of Mr. Lyford; she died there on 18 July 1817 at lodgings at No. 8 College Street, and was buried a few days later in the north aisle of Winchester Cathedral.
claims.clinical_interpretation: History only; not used in the modern episode.

claims.statement: The Jane Austen Society's biography says she fell ill in 1816, possibly with Addison's disease.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Retrospective interpretation; the modern episode makes this diagnosis as synthetic content, not as a claim about her.

claims.statement: In 1964 the surgeon Sir Zachary Cope proposed in the British Medical Journal that her final illness was Addison's disease, which in his time was usually tuberculous; he relied heavily on her description of her colouring.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Retrospective interpretation, disputed by later authors.

source_links.locator: initially identified by Sir Zachary Cope in 1964 as Addison's disease

claims.statement: Annette Upfal argued in 2005 that the evidence tends to exclude Addison's disease and that her fatal illness was quite possibly Hodgkin's disease, a lymphoma, with an immune deficiency perhaps present by January 1813; she also noted that Cassandra destroyed letters containing medical detail and that the cause cannot now be established conclusively.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Retrospective interpretation; the reason the modern consultant keeps lymphoma in the differential until it is excluded.

claims.statement: Katherine White argued in 2009 that symptoms reported by Addison's patients of the period (mental confusion, generalised pain, weight loss and anorexia) are absent from her letters, so Addison's disease is unlikely, and that disseminated bovine tuberculosis would explain her symptoms coherently.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Retrospective interpretation; the reason tuberculosis is considered as a cause until the antibody result is known.

claims.statement: Sanders and Graham argued in 2021 that the rheumatism, facial skin changes, fever and fluctuating symptoms in her letters fulfil current classification criteria for systemic lupus erythematosus.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Retrospective interpretation; not used in the modern episode.

claims.statement: A British Library curator noted in 2017 that her early death has been attributed to Addison's disease, cancer and tuberculosis, and that in 2011 a crime writer suggested arsenic poisoning on the basis of her facial pigmentation; the curator presented cataracts, possibly from arsenic, only as a theory raised by her spectacles.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Retrospective speculation; not used in the modern episode.

claims.statement: Her father died on 21 January 1805 after an illness of only forty-eight hours.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Family history; the cause is not recorded in the cited source.

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Recognize primary adrenal insufficiency in a 40-year-old writer whose tiredness, weight loss, nausea, back ache and darkening skin could be put down to overwork or low mood, and care for it on the Endocrine Society 2016 guideline: low sodium, high potassium and raised eosinophils as clues; urgent testing with an 8 am cortisol and ACTH and a cosyntropin stimulation test, without delaying treatment if she becomes unstable; renin and aldosterone for mineralocorticoid deficiency; 21-hydroxylase antibodies for the cause, with adrenal imaging and tuberculosis testing only if they are negative; lymphoma kept in the differential (examination for nodes and spleen, LDH, chest X-ray, and weight and symptoms on treatment) because a retrospective diagnosis of her real illness proposes it; hydrocortisone in two daily doses and fludrocortisone adjusted by blood pressure lying and standing, electrolytes and renin; written sick-day rules, an emergency injection kit, a steroid card and a medical ID, then used in a febrile illness; screening for associated autoimmune disease; anemia work-up (CMID anemia monograph); and listening to the patient's own written account of her illness. Her real illness remains undiagnosed; this record shows one modern possibility, not an answer.

hpi.narrative: Ms. Austen returns three days after her first visit and was seen this morning by Dr. Varga-Whitlock of endocrinology, who performed a cosyntropin stimulation test. Since her last visit she has salted her food freely and has felt about the same: tired, with little appetite, a bout of nausea each morning, and lightheadedness when she stands quickly. She vomited once two days ago but kept fluids down afterwards. She has had no fainting, confusion, or severe abdominal pain. Her back still aches by the end of the day. She has brought a page of notes on how she has felt each day since the winter.

referral.question: Suspected primary adrenal insufficiency in a 40-year-old novelist with about three months of tiredness, weight loss, darkening skin, nausea and back ache, a postural fall in blood pressure, low sodium, high potassium and raised eosinophils. Please confirm or exclude the diagnosis, start replacement if confirmed, and plan the search for the cause
referral.urgency: Urgent, within three days; she is stable today and has been told to go to the emergency department at once for vomiting, fainting, confusion or severe abdominal pain
referral.pertinent_history: Since the winter she has become steadily more tired, cutting her writing from full mornings to an hour or two, with poor appetite, morning nausea and occasional vomiting, a loss of 5 kg from her usual 57 kg, a dull low back ache by evening, salt craving, and lightheadedness on standing. She has noticed her face and hands darkening. She feels feverish on some evenings but has no drenching night sweats, cough, or lumps that she has noticed. She was very ill with a fever as a young child; no other serious illness. No medicines, including no corticosteroids by any route, and no known allergy. Today: weight 52.0 kg (BMI 18.0), blood pressure 98/62 seated with a postural fall, pulse 92, temperature 37.4 °C; bronze pigmentation of the face, hands, palmar creases and gums; no lymph nodes or enlarged spleen. Results today: sodium 131, potassium 5.4, chloride 99, bicarbonate 21 mmol/L, urea nitrogen 23 and creatinine 0.94 mg/dL, eGFR 79, glucose 72 mg/dL, calcium 10.1 mg/dL; hemoglobin 11.4 g/dL with MCV 89 fL, white cells 5.8 with eosinophils 0.74 x10^3/uL, platelets 262; TSH 3.6 mIU/L, free T4 1.1 ng/dL; ferritin 64 ng/mL, vitamin B12 486 pg/mL, folate 11.2 ng/mL. PHQ-9 6, carried by tiredness, appetite and sleep. She has brought written notes on her symptoms since the winter and would like them read
questions: Does she have primary adrenal insufficiency, and which tests confirm it?
Should replacement start at once, and at what doses of hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone?
How should the cause be established, and when are adrenal imaging and tuberculosis testing needed?
Should lymphoma be kept in the differential, given her weight loss and evening feverishness, and how should it be excluded?
What sick-day rules, emergency supplies and follow-up do you advise, including screening for associated autoimmune disease?

consultant_note.history: Ms. Austen, a 40-year-old novelist, is seen at the request of Dr. Pemberton-Okafor three days after her first visit. Her written notes trace a gradual decline since the winter: tiredness that is worst by afternoon, loss of appetite with morning nausea, a few episodes of vomiting, about 5 kg of weight loss, a dull ache in the low back by evening, salt craving, lightheadedness on standing, and darkening of her face and hands that friends have remarked on. She has felt feverish on some evenings without drenching sweats. She has had no cough, breathlessness, itching, or lumps. She takes no medicines and has never had corticosteroids by any route. Her periods are regular. No family history of adrenal, thyroid or autoimmune disease is known to her. She has been salting her food since her first visit and vomited once two days ago. She wants a clear explanation and to be able to manage the condition herself
consultant_note.data_reviewed: Dr. Pemberton-Okafor's intake note and results: sodium 131, potassium 5.4 mmol/L, bicarbonate 21 mmol/L, urea nitrogen 23 mg/dL, glucose 72 mg/dL; hemoglobin 11.4 g/dL, normocytic, with eosinophils 0.74 x10^3/uL; TSH 3.6 mIU/L; ferritin, vitamin B12 and folate normal. This morning, before any treatment: cortisol 2.6 ug/dL at 8 am with ACTH 548 pg/mL; after cosyntropin 250 mcg intravenously, cortisol 3.4 ug/dL at 30 minutes and 3.9 ug/dL at 60 minutes; plasma renin activity 16.2 ng/mL/h, aldosterone 1.8 ng/dL; sodium 132, potassium 5.3 mmol/L; LDH 172 U/L. Chest X-ray this morning: clear lungs, no hilar or mediastinal widening, no calcified nodes or other sign of old or active tuberculosis

exam.finding: Thin and tired but alert; weight 51.8 kg
100/64 lying, 86/56 standing, pulse 88 rising to 106
Diffuse bronze pigmentation of the face and hands, deepest in the palmar creases, knuckles and a forearm scar; brown patches on the gums and buccal mucosa; no vitiligo
No cervical, supraclavicular, axillary or inguinal nodes
No enlarged liver or spleen; no tenderness
Thyroid normal size, no nodules

assessment.assessment: Confirmed. Cortisol does not rise after cosyntropin (peak 3.9 ug/dL, against a threshold of 18), and the ACTH of 548 pg/mL shows the failure is in the adrenal glands rather than the pituitary. The high renin with low aldosterone shows mineralocorticoid deficiency too, which accounts for the low sodium, high potassium, salt craving and postural drop. The pigmentation, the raised eosinophils, the mild anemia and the back ache all fit. Treatment should start today without waiting for the cause

In a woman of 40 in this country autoimmune adrenalitis is by far the commonest cause, and 21-hydroxylase antibodies will show it in most cases. If they are negative, the adrenal glands should be imaged by CT to look for enlargement or calcification, and tuberculosis tested for, because tuberculosis remains the main infectious cause worldwide. Lymphoma can rarely infiltrate both adrenals, and her weight loss and evening feverishness deserve to be taken seriously; but with no nodes or enlarged spleen, a normal LDH and blood count apart from the eosinophils, and a normal chest X-ray, it is unlikely. Low-grade feverishness and weight loss are common in untreated adrenal insufficiency and should settle on replacement; if they do not, or if nodes appear, CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis is needed
With normal iron, vitamin B12 and folate, this is the anemia of untreated adrenal insufficiency and should recover on replacement

recommendations: Start hydrocortisone today: 10 mg on waking and 5 mg at 2 pm (15 mg a day), adjusted by weight, energy, appetite, pigmentation and blood pressure rather than by cortisol levels

Start fludrocortisone 0.1 mg each morning; check sodium and potassium at two weeks and renin with lying and standing blood pressure at about six weeks, aiming for renin in the upper normal range; she should salt food to taste
21-hydroxylase antibodies at the two-week visit (they are not affected by treatment); adrenal CT and tuberculosis testing only if they are negative

Keep lymphoma in the differential until weight and symptoms have recovered: weight, fevers, night sweats, lymph nodes and spleen at each visit, and CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis if weight loss, fevers or nodes persist once replacement is established

Sick-day rules: double the hydrocortisone for fever above 38 °C and triple it above 39 °C until a day after the fever settles; inject 100 mg into the thigh and call 911 for vomiting, inability to take tablets, or feeling faint. For surgery under general anesthesia or a major illness in hospital, hydrocortisone 100 mg intravenously at induction and then 200 mg a day until she is eating, tapering back over one to two days
An emergency hydrocortisone injection kit with training today, a steroid emergency card, a medical ID, and a written emergency letter

Screen for associated autoimmune disease: TSH (normal today) at least yearly; A1c and celiac serology with total IgA at the two-week visit, and vitamin B12 (normal at intake) yearly; ask about periods at each visit and check FSH if they become irregular or stop
Repeat the blood count at two and six weeks; no further anemia work-up unless it fails to recover
consultant_note.communication: Discussed with Dr. Pemberton-Okafor, who sees her the same day, and the first doses were taken in clinic. The diagnosis, the reason for lifelong replacement and the sick-day rules were explained to Ms. Austen, who asked careful questions, read through the written rules, and gave a practice injection on a trainer
consultant_note.follow_up: Endocrinology review in one year, or sooner for an adrenal crisis, negative antibodies, or symptoms that do not settle; Dr. Pemberton-Okafor continues prescribing and monitoring and will share the two- and six-week results
